   - A 60-year-old postmenopausal woman with 1 year of severe vulvar pruritus and progressive dyspareunia: the leading etiologies in this age group are hypoestrogenic genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM/atrophic vulvovaginitis) and chronic vulvar dermatoses (especially lichen sclerosus). GSM commonly causes dryness, burning, itch and pain with intercourse in postmenopausal women. Lichen sclerosus is classically associated with chronic intense pruritus in older women and can cause scarring and dyspareunia, even when the patient has not noticed obvious white patches. Allergic/irritant contact dermatitis or chronic eczema can also produce longstanding vulvar itching and secondary pain with intercourse. Less likely (but considered if biopsy/exam suggest) are infectious causes (recurrent candidiasis), lichen planus/erosive disease, or neoplastic processes — these are best evaluated if biopsy or examination raises concern. The ranking reflects pretest probabilities given age, chronicity, and symptom pattern.

[CANDIDATES]
1. Genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM; atrophic vulvovaginitis)
   - Gold Standard: Objective evidence of atrophic changes — vaginal cytology showing predominance of parabasal cells with reduced superficial cells plus clinical exam showing pale, thin, friable vulvovaginal mucosa and elevated vaginal pH (>5). (Clinical diagnosis supported by these objective findings and symptomatic response to topical estrogen.)

2. Lichen sclerosus (vulvar)
   - Gold Standard: Vulvar biopsy with characteristic histopathology (thinned epidermis/epithelial atrophy, loss of rete ridges, homogenization of collagen in the upper dermis, and a lichenoid inflammatory infiltrate) confirming diagnosis and excluding VIN/malignancy.

3. Vulvar dermatitis (allergic or irritant contact dermatitis / chronic eczematous dermatitis)
   - Gold Standard: Positive vulvar patch testing identifying a relevant allergen that reproduces dermatitis + clinical correlation (improvement after avoidance of the identified allergen). If uncertain, biopsy can help distinguish from inflammatory dermatoses.

[DIFFERENTIAL_EVIDENCE]
1. Focused vulvar and speculum examination (including colposcopic inspection) — presence of porcelain-white, atrophic plaques, fissures, scarring or architectural distortion (labial fusion/introital narrowing) supports lichen sclerosus; diffuse pale, thin mucosa with loss of rugae and vaginal dryness supports GSM; erythema, vesiculation or eczematous scale suggests contact dermatitis or eczema.

2. Vulvar biopsy histopathology — will distinguish lichen sclerosus or lichen planus or VIN/cancer (biopsy diagnostic for LS or LP; neoplasia excluded/confirmed), and is indicated when appearance is atypical, if there are erosions, persistent unexplained lesions, or poor response to empiric therapy.

3. Vaginal/cervicovaginal testing — vaginal pH measurement and vaginal cytology (wet mount/Papanicolaou or cytology showing parabasal cells) and KOH/prep or fungal culture/PCR: parabasal-cell–predominant cytology with elevated pH supports GSM; positive KOH budding hyphae or fungal culture supports chronic candidiasis; absence of infective organisms points away from infectious causes.

4. Patch testing and therapeutic trials — positive vulvar patch testing to a relevant allergen supports allergic contact dermatitis; trial of high‑potency topical corticosteroid (e.g., clobetasol) with clinical response supports lichen sclerosus or inflammatory dermatosis, whereas trial of topical vaginal estrogen with symptomatic and exam improvement supports GSM.
